short: A traditional South Asian weight unit for gold and silver, equal to about 11.66 grams, though Indians often loosely call 10 grams a tola.
kid: A tola is a little measuring weight for gold, like a small scoop for measuring sugar. Grandma might say she has five tolas of gold, meaning five scoops of it.
detail: The tola is a traditional unit of mass used for gold and silver across South Asia and in the Gulf bullion trade. In 1833 British India standardised it at 180 grains, or 11.6638 grams, the weight of a silver rupee coin. India switched to metric units from 1958, and Indian jewellers and exchanges such as MCX now quote gold per 10 grams. Many people still call 10 grams 'one tola', so an Indian 'tola rate' usually means the 10-gram price. Pakistan and Nepal, by contrast, quote gold per true tola of 11.66 grams, and the popular ten-tola bar sold in Dubai and South Asia weighs 116.64 grams, or 3.75 troy ounces. The common mistake is comparing a Pakistani or Nepali per-tola price with an Indian per-10-gram price: the true tola is about 16.6% heavier, so adjust for weight and currency first.
example: Say gold costs ₹10,000 per gram. A 10-gram 'tola' quote would be ₹1,00,000, but a true tola of 11.66 grams would cost 11.66 × ₹10,000 = ₹1,16,600, a gap of ₹16,600.
formula: 1 tola = 180 grains = 11.6638 grams; 8 tolas = 3 troy ounces

short: How many ounces of silver it takes to buy one ounce of gold, found by dividing the gold price by the silver price.
kid: If one shiny gold sticker can be swapped for 80 silver stickers, the swap number is 80. When gold stickers become more special, you need even more silver ones.
detail: The gold-silver ratio divides the price of an ounce of gold by the price of an ounce of silver, telling you how many ounces of silver one ounce of gold buys. Traders use it to judge which precious metal looks relatively cheap. The two metals usually move together, but silver is more volatile because roughly half of its demand is industrial, from solar panels, electronics and vehicles, while gold is driven mainly by investors, jewellery and central banks. So the ratio tends to rise in recessions and panics, briefly topping 120 in March 2020, and to fall when industry is booming. When governments fixed both metals' prices in the 19th century, the ratio was held near 15 or 16. Two cautions: there is no natural level the ratio must return to, and in India you must convert units first, since MCX quotes gold per 10 grams but silver per kilogram.
example: Say gold trades at $2,000 an ounce and silver at $25. The ratio is 2,000 / 25 = 80, so one ounce of gold buys 80 ounces of silver. If silver rises to $40 while gold stays at $2,000, the ratio falls to 50.
formula: Gold-silver ratio = Price of gold per ounce / Price of silver per ounce

short: Gold bought in small amounts on an app and stored in the seller's vault; as of 2025, neither SEBI nor RBI regulates it in India.
kid: You give a shop a few coins, and they put a tiny piece of gold in their big safe with your name on it. You cannot hold it, but you can ask for it later.
detail: Digital gold lets you buy 24-carat gold online in tiny amounts, often for a few rupees, through apps. The app partners with a provider that buys an equal amount of physical gold and stores it in an insured vault, often overseen by an independent trustee. You can later sell it back or take delivery as coins or bars, paying making and delivery charges. Buy and sell prices differ, so short holding periods usually lose money. Under the rules as of 2025, each purchase attracts 3% GST, and digital gold is neither a security nor a deposit, so neither SEBI nor RBI supervises it; SEBI barred brokers from selling it in 2021 and warned investors again in 2025. Regulated alternatives include gold ETFs, gold mutual funds and Electronic Gold Receipts. 'Digital gold' is also a nickname for Bitcoin, an entirely different asset.
example: Say gold is ₹10,000 per gram and you pay ₹1,030: ₹30 is 3% GST and ₹1,000 buys 0.1 gram. If the platform's buy-back price is 3% lower, at ₹9,700 per gram, selling at once returns 0.1 × ₹9,700 = ₹970, a loss of ₹60.

short: Purchases of gold by national central banks to hold in their official reserves, a major source of global gold demand since 2010.
kid: A country's big money keeper puts some shiny gold in its safe, just in case. Gold stays special even when other things get wobbly.
detail: Central banks hold gold as part of their foreign exchange reserves because it carries no default risk, cannot be printed by another government and tends to hold value in crises. After two decades as net sellers, central banks became net buyers in 2010, and purchases jumped after Western countries froze Russia's reserves in 2022, showing that dollar and euro assets can be blocked. According to the World Gold Council, they bought more than 1,000 tonnes in each of 2022, 2023 and 2024, around a fifth of global demand. Large buyers have included China, Poland, Turkey and India; the RBI also brought about 100 tonnes home from the Bank of England in 2024. Because these buyers are steady and largely price-insensitive, their demand supports gold prices. Do not confuse this with a gold standard: buying gold diversifies reserves, but it does not tie the currency's value to gold.
example: Say a central bank holds $600 billion of reserves, of which $60 billion (10%) is gold. If it swaps $30 billion of US Treasuries for gold, its gold rises to $90 billion, or 15% of the same $600 billion total.
formula: Gold share of reserves = Value of gold holdings / Total foreign exchange reserves

short: Official certification of the purity of gold or silver jewellery; in India, a BIS mark plus a unique six-character HUID code on each piece.
kid: A hallmark is a tiny stamp on a gold ring that says the gold is real and as pure as promised. It is like a teacher's tick showing your work was checked.
detail: Hallmarking is the official certification of the purity, or fineness, of precious metal articles. In India it is run by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) through licensed Assaying and Hallmarking Centres, which test samples and laser-mark each piece. Hallmarking of gold jewellery became mandatory in phases from June 2021, starting with 256 districts and later extended to more. Since April 2023 each hallmarked piece must carry three marks: the BIS logo, a purity grade such as 22K916 or 18K750, and a six-character alphanumeric Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID), which buyers can verify on the BIS Care app. Hallmarking protects buyers from under-karatage, where jewellery is sold as purer than it is, and has helped organised jewellers gain share from unorganised ones. The common confusion: a hallmark certifies purity only, not weight, price or making charges, and 22 carat means 91.6% gold, not pure gold.
example: A 10-gram chain stamped 22K916 contains 10 × 0.916 = 9.16 grams of pure gold. If pure gold is, say, ₹10,000 a gram, the gold content is worth ₹91,600 before making charges and GST.
formula: Pure gold content = Gross weight × Fineness (e.g. 916/1000 for 22 carat)

short: A reddish industrial metal used in wiring, motors and plumbing; its price is watched as a gauge of global economic health.
kid: Copper is the shiny orange metal inside wires that carry electricity to your lights. When lots of new houses and toys are being built, everyone wants more copper.
detail: Copper is a highly conductive metal used in power cables, wiring, motors, plumbing and electronics. Electric vehicles, renewable power and grid upgrades use far more copper than older technologies, which makes it central to the energy transition. China consumes more than half of the world's refined copper, while Chile is the largest miner, with Peru and the Democratic Republic of Congo among the next largest. Benchmark prices are set on the London Metal Exchange in dollars per tonne and on COMEX in dollars per pound; in India, MCX copper futures trade in rupees per kilogram. Copper earned the nickname 'Dr. Copper' because its price often turns before the wider economy does. Treat that signal with care: mine strikes, Chinese stockpiling or tariff fears can move copper without any change in global growth. India became a net importer of refined copper after the Sterlite smelter in Thoothukudi shut in 2018.
example: COMEX quotes copper in dollars per pound and the LME in dollars per tonne. Since a tonne is 2,204.62 pounds, a COMEX price of, say, $4.50 a pound equals 4.50 × 2,204.62 = about $9,921 a tonne.
formula: Price per tonne = Price per pound × 2,204.62

short: A light, rust-resistant industrial metal used in cars, aircraft, cans, packaging and power lines; making it takes huge amounts of electricity.
kid: Aluminium is the light, silvery metal in drink cans and kitchen foil. It is easy to carry and can be melted down and used again and again.
detail: Aluminium is the most widely used non-ferrous metal, prized for being light, strong and resistant to corrosion. It goes into vehicles, aircraft, buildings, power transmission lines and packaging. Production has two stages: bauxite ore is refined into alumina, and alumina is smelted into metal by electrolysis, which consumes roughly 14 megawatt-hours of electricity per tonne. That makes power the biggest cost and makes coal-based smelters carbon-intensive, a growing issue under the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. China produces close to 60% of the world's primary aluminium, and India is the second-largest producer. The global benchmark is the LME price in dollars per tonne, but buyers also pay regional premiums for delivery, so the LME price alone understates actual cost. Recycling saves about 95% of the energy. Aluminium and aluminum are the same metal: the first is the British and Indian spelling, the second American.
example: Say a smelter uses 14 MWh of electricity per tonne of aluminium and pays $50 per MWh. Power then costs 14 × $50 = $700 per tonne; if the power price doubles to $100, the power bill rises to $1,400 per tonne.

short: Common industrial metals such as copper, aluminium, zinc, nickel, lead and tin, as opposed to precious metals like gold and silver.
kid: Base metals are the everyday metals that build cars, wires and pots. Gold is the fancy jewellery metal; base metals are the hard-working helpers.
detail: Base metals are common, non-precious metals that corrode or oxidise relatively easily, unlike gold, silver and platinum. The main traded ones are copper, aluminium, zinc, nickel, lead and tin, all benchmarked on the London Metal Exchange. In market usage they are also called non-ferrous metals because they contain no significant iron; iron ore and steel are usually tracked separately. Demand comes from construction, power grids, vehicles, machinery and batteries, so prices track industrial activity, especially in China, which uses about half of the world's supply of most of them. In India, MCX offers futures on copper, aluminium, zinc, lead and nickel, and listed metal producers' earnings swing with LME prices and the rupee. A common confusion: in jewellery, base metal means the cheaper metal under a gold or silver plating, which is a different usage from the commodity-market term.
example: Say a hypothetical zinc miner, XYZ Ltd, sells 1 million tonnes a year. If the LME zinc price rises by $200 a tonne, its annual revenue rises by 1,000,000 × $200 = $200 million, before any change in costs.

short: Rock rich in iron that is mined and used almost entirely to make steel; a key export for Australia, Brazil and India.
kid: Iron ore is a heavy reddish rock dug from the ground. Big hot ovens melt it to make steel for bridges, buildings and cars.
detail: Iron ore is rock containing iron oxides, and about 98% of what is mined ends up in steel, made in blast furnaces with coking coal or through direct reduction. Australia and Brazil dominate seaborne exports, while China buys roughly 70% of seaborne ore, so Chinese property and infrastructure activity largely sets the price. The benchmark is fines with 62% iron content delivered to northern China, with futures on the Singapore Exchange and China's Dalian Commodity Exchange. Higher-grade ore and pellets earn premiums because they need less energy and produce fewer emissions. India is a major producer, with mines in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Karnataka; it raised the export duty on iron ore to 50% in May 2022 to keep ore at home for steelmakers, then removed it for lower grades six months later. Do not confuse ore prices with steel prices: steelmakers' profit depends on the gap between the two.
example: Benchmark prices assume 62% iron content. Say 62% fines sell at $100 a tonne and a 58% cargo is priced in proportion to its iron: it would fetch $100 × 58 / 62 = about $93.55 a tonne, though real low-grade discounts are often steeper.

short: A very light metal that is the key ingredient in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries for phones, electric vehicles and grid storage.
kid: Lithium is a tiny, light metal hiding inside batteries. It helps phones and electric cars store power so they can keep going.
detail: Lithium is the lightest metal and the key element in lithium-ion batteries for phones, electric vehicles and grid storage; with nickel, cobalt and graphite it is often called a battery metal. It is extracted from hard-rock spodumene, mainly in Australia, and from salt-flat brines in Chile and Argentina, then refined into lithium carbonate or hydroxide, mostly in China, which handles roughly two-thirds of chemical processing. Prices are volatile because new supply arrives in lumps: Chinese lithium carbonate prices rose more than tenfold between 2020 and late 2022, then fell over 80% by 2024. Most lithium is sold under contracts, with futures on the Guangzhou Futures Exchange and CME. India imports nearly all its needs; in 2023 the Geological Survey of India reported an inferred resource of 5.9 million tonnes in Jammu and Kashmir. Confusion to avoid: an inferred resource is an early estimate, not a proven, mineable reserve.
example: Lithium is often measured as lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE). Since lithium makes up about 18.8% of lithium carbonate by weight, 1 tonne of lithium metal equals about 1 / 0.188 = 5.32 tonnes of LCE.
formula: Lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) = Lithium metal content × 5.323

short: A group of 17 metals, including neodymium and dysprosium, vital for powerful magnets in electric motors, wind turbines, electronics and defence systems.
kid: Rare earths are special pinches of metal that make super-strong tiny magnets. Those magnets help toy cars, fans and phones buzz and spin.
detail: Rare earth elements are 17 metals: the 15 lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium. Despite the name, they are not especially rare in the Earth's crust; what is rare is finding them in rich deposits, and separating them from one another is chemically difficult and polluting. Neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium go into permanent magnets for electric-vehicle motors, wind turbines, electronics and missiles. China mines around two-thirds of the world's rare earths and does about 90% of refining and magnet making, which gives it leverage: in April 2025 it required export licences for seven rare earths and related magnets, causing shortages at carmakers worldwide, including in India. India has sizeable monazite beach-sand deposits, processed by the state-owned IREL. A common confusion: lithium, cobalt and nickel are critical minerals but not rare earths.
example: Say a hypothetical carmaker, ABC Motors, needs 1 kg of rare-earth magnets per electric car and plans 50,000 cars. It needs 50,000 kg, or 50 tonnes, of magnets; if export licences hold up 40% of supply, output of 20,000 cars is at risk.

short: Minerals a country considers essential to its economy or security but whose supply is at risk, such as lithium, cobalt, graphite and rare earths.
kid: Critical minerals are special rocks a country really needs to make batteries, phones and machines. If only one faraway place has them, the country worries about running out.
detail: Critical minerals are a policy category, not a chemical one: each government lists the minerals it considers vital to its economy, energy transition or defence and whose supply is concentrated or vulnerable. Lists commonly include lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, rare earths, gallium and germanium, and sometimes copper. India's Ministry of Mines named 30 critical minerals in 2023 and launched the National Critical Mineral Mission in 2025 to fund exploration, auctions of mining blocks, recycling and overseas assets through the state-backed KABIL. Supply is highly concentrated: the Democratic Republic of Congo mines about 70% of the world's cobalt, Indonesia over half of its nickel, and China refines most of these minerals. That makes them a tool of geopolitics, appearing in export controls, trade deals and subsidies. Confusion to avoid: critical does not mean scarce, and lists change as technologies and suppliers change.
example: Say a country imports 90% of a mineral it uses, and 80% of those imports come from one supplier. That supplier then provides 0.9 × 0.8 = 72% of total use, which is why the mineral would score high on supply risk.

short: Raw farm products traded in bulk, such as wheat, rice, soybeans, sugar, coffee, cotton and livestock, whose prices hinge on weather and harvests.
kid: These are the things farmers grow or raise, like wheat for bread and sugar for sweets. If it rains just right, there is lots to share; if not, there is less.
detail: Agricultural commodities are raw farm products traded in bulk on spot markets and futures exchanges. Traders group them into grains and oilseeds, such as wheat, corn, rice and soybeans; softs, mostly tropical and fibre crops such as sugar, coffee, cocoa and cotton; and livestock. Prices depend on weather, including India's monsoon and El Niño, plus planted area, stock levels, biofuel demand and government policy. Global benchmarks trade on Chicago's CBOT and on ICE. In India, NCDEX and MCX list farm futures, but SEBI suspended futures in seven sensitive commodities, including wheat, chana, soybean and crude palm oil, in December 2021, a ban still in force under the rules as of 2025. Policy tools such as minimum support prices and export bans, like India's 2022 wheat export ban, can matter as much as harvests. Do not equate farm-gate prices with retail food inflation, which also reflects transport, processing and margins.
example: Say a farmer expects 50 quintals of jeera and sells NCDEX futures at ₹25,000 per quintal. If the price falls to ₹22,000 by harvest, the futures gain is ₹3,000 × 50 = ₹1,50,000, offsetting the lower price he gets for his crop.

short: Cooking oils such as palm, soybean, sunflower and mustard oil; India imports most of its needs, so world prices quickly reach Indian kitchens.
kid: Edible oil is the oil we cook food in, like when frying puris. A lot of it comes from faraway farms, so when it costs more there, the oil in our kitchen costs more too.
detail: Edible oils include palm, soybean, sunflower, mustard, groundnut and rice bran oil. India is the world's largest importer of vegetable oils, buying roughly 15 to 16 million tonnes a year, well over half of its consumption. Palm oil comes mainly from Indonesia and Malaysia, soybean oil from Argentina and Brazil, and sunflower oil from Russia and Ukraine. Prices respond to crop yields, crude oil (palm and soybean oil also feed biodiesel), exporters' policies such as Indonesia's brief palm oil export ban in 2022, and the rupee. India's main lever is import duty: it cuts duties when prices spike and raises them to protect oilseed farmers, as in September 2024, before partly reversing in May 2025. Benchmarks include Bursa Malaysia palm oil futures and CBOT soybean oil. Confusion to avoid: the duty gap between crude and refined oil decides whether India imports raw oil for local refining or finished oil.
example: Say crude palm oil lands at ₹90,000 per tonne before duty. With an assumed effective import duty of 16.5%, the landed cost is ₹90,000 × 1.165 = ₹1,04,850; halving the duty to 8.25% cuts it to ₹97,425.
formula: Landed cost = Import price × (1 + Effective import duty rate)

short: Mixing ethanol, an alcohol made from sugarcane or grain, into petrol; India's programme reached 20% blending, called E20, in 2025.
kid: It is like mixing a little liquid made from sugarcane into the petrol for cars. That way the country needs less petrol from far away, and farmers sell more sugarcane.
detail: Ethanol blending means mixing ethanol, an alcohol made by fermenting sugarcane juice, molasses or grains such as maize and rice, into petrol. Under India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) programme, oil marketing companies buy ethanol from distilleries at government-set prices and blend it at depots. Blending rose from about 1.5% in 2014 to about 20% in 2025, five years ahead of the original 2030 target for E20. The goals are to cut crude oil imports, save foreign exchange, lower emissions and support farmers and sugar mills, which now earn steady revenue from ethanol. Side effects include sugar diverted from food, higher maize prices, and debates over water use and older vehicles' mileage, since ethanol carries about a third less energy per litre than petrol. Brazil runs far higher blends. Confusion to avoid: blend percentages are by volume, and blending does not automatically make pump prices cheaper.
example: Say a state sells 10 crore litres of E20 petrol a month: 20%, or 2 crore litres, is ethanol. That displaces 2 crore litres of petrol by volume, but because ethanol carries about a third less energy per litre, the real saving in petrol is smaller.
formula: Blend rate = Ethanol volume / (Ethanol volume + Petrol volume)

short: India's largest commodity derivatives exchange, based in Mumbai, where futures and options on gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas and base metals trade.
kid: MCX is like a big market hall where grown-ups agree today on the price of gold or oil they will swap later. Everyone follows the same rules so nobody gets cheated.
detail: The Multi Commodity Exchange of India (MCX), set up in 2003 and based in Mumbai, is the country's dominant commodity derivatives exchange, handling, as of 2025, well over 90% of commodity futures and options turnover. It lists contracts on bullion (gold and silver), energy (crude oil and natural gas) and base metals, plus a few farm products such as cotton. Trading runs from 9 am until late at night, overlapping US trading hours. Since 2015, when the Forward Markets Commission merged into SEBI, MCX has been regulated by SEBI, and its trades are cleared by its subsidiary MCX Clearing Corporation. MCX prices track international benchmarks converted into rupees plus import duties; its crude oil and natural gas contracts settle against NYMEX prices. Confusion to avoid: the exchange is also a listed company, so buying MCX shares is a bet on the exchange's business, not on commodity prices.
example: MCX's standard gold futures contract covers 1 kg but is quoted per 10 grams. Say the price is ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams: one contract is worth 100 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹1 crore, and a 1% move changes its value by ₹1 lakh.

short: An Indian exchange, based in Mumbai, that specialises in futures on farm products such as guar, jeera, turmeric, cottonseed oilcake and castor seed.
kid: NCDEX is a market where farmers and traders agree on prices for crops like cumin and turmeric before harvest. It helps a farmer know what the crop will bring.
detail: The National Commodity and Derivatives Exchange (NCDEX), launched in 2003 and based in Mumbai, is India's main exchange for agricultural commodity futures. Its founding shareholders included LIC, NABARD, NSE and ICICI Bank. It lists contracts on spices, oilseeds, guar and cotton products, most of which settle by physical delivery through accredited warehouses, so its prices reflect real crop stocks. Like MCX, it is regulated by SEBI. Farmer Producer Organisations and processors use it to hedge, and its prices guide traders in physical mandis. Its volumes fell sharply after SEBI suspended futures in seven key farm commodities, including wheat, chana and soybean, in December 2021, a ban still in force under the rules as of 2025. Agricultural futures are politically sensitive because they are often blamed, sometimes without evidence, for food inflation. Confusion to avoid: NCDEX handles only a small slice of India's commodity derivatives turnover; MCX dominates.
example: Say a farmer producer organisation expects 100 tonnes of turmeric and sells NCDEX futures at ₹14,000 per quintal. Since 100 tonnes is 1,000 quintals, it has roughly locked in 1,000 × ₹14,000 = ₹1.4 crore before costs, whatever the spot price at harvest.

short: The world's main exchange for industrial metals such as copper, aluminium, zinc and nickel, whose prices serve as global benchmarks.
kid: The LME is a very old market in London where people agree prices for metals like copper. Lots of countries use its prices as the starting point.
detail: The London Metal Exchange (LME), founded in 1877 and owned by Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing since 2012, is the world's main market for industrial metals: copper, aluminium, zinc, nickel, lead, tin and cobalt. Its prices, in dollars per tonne, are the reference for physical supply contracts worldwide, including sales by Indian producers. Unusual features include daily delivery dates out to three months, with the three-month contract as the headline benchmark; the Ring, Europe's last open-outcry trading floor; and a global network of approved warehouses whose stock levels traders watch as a supply signal. In March 2022 a short squeeze sent nickel above $100,000 a tonne, and the LME suspended trading and cancelled billions of dollars of trades, damaging its reputation. Confusion to avoid: the LME handles base metals, while gold and silver benchmarks run through the separate London Bullion Market Association.
example: LME copper trades in lots of 25 tonnes. Say copper is $9,000 a tonne: one lot is worth 25 × $9,000 = $225,000, and a $100 move in the price changes the lot's value by $2,500.

short: A Chicago-based exchange group that runs the world's biggest futures markets, including benchmark contracts for US crude oil, gold, grains and interest rates.
kid: CME is a giant market in Chicago where people promise today to buy or sell things like corn or gold later at a set price. It makes sure everyone keeps their promise.
detail: CME Group, headquartered in Chicago, is the world's largest derivatives marketplace. It formed in 2007 when the Chicago Mercantile Exchange merged with the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT), and added the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) and its metals division COMEX in 2008. Its contracts set global benchmarks: WTI crude oil and Henry Hub natural gas on NYMEX; gold, silver and copper on COMEX; corn, wheat, soybeans and US Treasury futures on CBOT; and S&P 500, SOFR and currency futures on CME. Most trading happens on its Globex electronic platform, and CME Clearing stands between buyers and sellers. It is regulated by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and its FedWatch tool turns Fed funds futures into rate-cut odds. Indian link: MCX crude oil and natural gas contracts settle against NYMEX prices. Confusion to avoid: Brent crude futures trade mainly on ICE, not CME.
example: One NYMEX WTI crude oil futures contract covers 1,000 barrels. Say the price rises from $70 to $72 a barrel: a buyer of one contract gains 1,000 × $2 = $2,000, and the seller loses the same amount.

short: The US government agency that regulates futures, options and swaps markets, including commodity, interest-rate and currency derivatives, to prevent fraud and manipulation.
kid: The CFTC is like a referee for a big American swapping game. It watches the players and blows the whistle if someone cheats.
detail: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is an independent US agency created in 1974 to regulate futures and options markets. Since the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 it also oversees most over-the-counter swaps. It supervises exchanges such as CME, clearing houses and brokers, and polices fraud, manipulation and spoofing; it fined several global banks for rigging LIBOR and currency benchmarks. Its weekly Commitments of Traders (COT) report, released on Fridays with data as of Tuesday, shows how commercial hedgers and speculators such as hedge funds are positioned, and traders read it for crowded bets in gold, oil or Treasury futures. As of 2025, the CFTC treats Bitcoin and Ether as commodities. Confusion to avoid: the CFTC regulates derivatives, while the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regulates stocks, bonds and other securities. In India, a single regulator, SEBI, covers both after absorbing the Forward Markets Commission in 2015.
example: Say the CFTC's Commitments of Traders report shows money managers holding 200,000 long and 50,000 short gold futures contracts. Their net long position is 200,000 - 50,000 = 150,000 contracts; at 100 troy ounces each, that is a net bet on 15 million ounces.
formula: Net position = Long contracts - Short contracts

short: India's largest power exchange, where electricity distribution companies, generators and big industrial users buy and sell electricity for the next day or hour.
kid: IEX is a market where electricity is bought and sold, like vegetables at a stall. When lots of people switch on fans on a hot day, the price goes up.
detail: The Indian Energy Exchange (IEX), operating since 2008, is India's largest power exchange, with the large majority of exchange-traded electricity volume; smaller rivals are Power Exchange India and Hindustan Power Exchange. It is regulated by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), not SEBI, although IEX Ltd's shares are listed. Its main products are the Day-Ahead Market, where power for each of the next day's 96 fifteen-minute blocks is priced by auction, and the Real-Time Market, with auctions every half hour, plus term-ahead, green power and renewable energy certificate markets. Exchanges handle under a tenth of India's electricity; most still flows through long-term power purchase agreements. Prices spike on hot summer evenings, and under the rules as of 2025 CERC caps the main markets at ₹10 per kWh. CERC's 2025 move towards market coupling, which pools bids across exchanges, is seen as a challenge to IEX's dominance.
example: IEX prices are quoted in rupees per megawatt-hour. Say a state distribution company buys 100 MW for one 15-minute block at ₹5,000 per MWh: it receives 100 × 0.25 = 25 MWh and pays 25 × ₹5,000 = ₹1,25,000.

short: A decade-or-longer stretch when prices of many raw materials stay well above trend because demand surges faster than new supply can arrive.
kid: Imagine all the kids in town suddenly want to build sandcastles, but there are only a few sand trucks. Sand stays hard to get for years, until more trucks come.
detail: A commodity super-cycle is a long upswing in the inflation-adjusted prices of a broad range of raw materials, lasting a decade or more, followed by a long downswing. Ordinary commodity cycles last a few years, but super-cycles are driven by structural demand shifts, such as a large economy industrialising. Because new mines, oilfields and plantations take five to fifteen years to develop, supply cannot catch up quickly, so prices stay high until new capacity arrives and then pushes them down for years. Economists have linked past super-cycles to US industrialisation, post-war reconstruction and China's boom from about 2000, when copper rose more than sixfold from its early-2000s lows to its 2011 peak. Analysts now debate whether the energy transition will drive another. For India, a big commodity importer, super-cycles usually mean higher inflation and wider trade deficits. Confusion to avoid: a one-year price spike is not a super-cycle.
example: Say a commodity index starts at 100 and rises 15% a year for 8 years. It ends at 100 × 1.15^8 = about 306, more than tripling, the kind of sustained rise people call a super-cycle.

short: A benchmark that tracks the prices of a basket of raw materials, such as oil, metals and crops, showing how commodities move overall.
kid: Imagine a basket with a little rice, a little oil and a little metal. If the whole basket costs more this week, the number goes up.
detail: A commodity index measures the combined price performance of a basket of raw materials. The best known are the Bloomberg Commodity Index (BCOM), which caps any single commodity at 15% and any sector at 33% to stay diversified; the S&P GSCI, weighted by world production, so energy often makes up more than half; and the CRB index, the oldest, dating from 1957. MCX publishes its own iCOMDEX indices for Indian markets. Most commodity indices are built from futures, not physical goods, so their total return has three parts: the change in spot prices, roll yield from swapping expiring contracts for later ones, and interest on the cash held as collateral. Investors use index funds to diversify and hedge inflation. Confusion to avoid: when later contracts cost more than near ones (contango), rolling loses money, so an index can lag the spot prices of the very commodities it tracks.
example: Say an index holds 60% energy, 25% metals and 15% crops. If energy rises 10%, metals fall 4% and crops are flat, the index moves 0.6 × 10% + 0.25 × (-4%) + 0.15 × 0% = +5%.
formula: Index return = Sum of (Weight of each commodity × Return of that commodity)

short: A daily index of the cost of hiring ships that carry dry bulk cargo, such as iron ore, coal and grain, across the oceans.
kid: Big ships carry rocks and grain across the sea, and you pay to borrow one. When lots of people want ships at once, borrowing one costs more, and this number goes up.
detail: The Baltic Dry Index (BDI), published every working day by London's Baltic Exchange, tracks the cost of hiring ships that carry dry bulk cargo such as iron ore, coal, grain and bauxite. It is a weighted average of daily time-charter rates for three ship sizes, Capesize (40%), Panamax (30%) and Supramax (30%), across major routes. Because the number of ships is fixed in the short run and new vessels take two to three years to build, small changes in demand cause big swings: the BDI hit a record 11,793 in May 2008 and crashed to 663 by December 2008. Traders watch it as an early signal of raw-material demand, especially from China. Confusion to avoid: the BDI covers only dry bulk, not container ships or oil tankers, and rates also move with fleet size, port congestion and route disruptions, so it is not a pure measure of the economy.
example: Say an importer charters a Capesize ship for 30 days at $20,000 a day to carry 180,000 tonnes of iron ore. The hire costs 30 × $20,000 = $600,000, or about $3.33 a tonne; if rates double to $40,000 a day, freight rises to about $6.67 a tonne.

short: The London trade body for the wholesale gold and silver market; it sets standards for bars and oversees the benchmark gold and silver prices.
kid: Imagine a club of grown-ups who check that every gold brick is real and weighs the right amount. Every day they also help agree on one fair price for gold.
detail: The London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), formed in 1987, is the trade body for London's wholesale gold and silver market, where banks and dealers trade directly with each other and store metal in vaults including the Bank of England's. It keeps the Good Delivery List of refiners whose bars meet strict standards, such as gold bars of about 400 troy ounces and at least 99.5% purity. Its benchmarks, the LBMA Gold Price, set twice daily by electronic auction, and the LBMA Silver Price, set once a day, are run by ICE Benchmark Administration and used to value ETFs, central bank deals and supply contracts. The gold auction replaced the century-old London gold fix in 2015. Confusion to avoid: the LBMA price is for metal in London, while COMEX futures are for New York delivery, and the gap can widen, as during the tariff scare of early 2025.
example: A London Good Delivery gold bar weighs about 400 troy ounces. Say gold is $2,000 an ounce: one bar is worth 400 × $2,000 = $800,000, and at 31.1035 grams an ounce it weighs about 12.44 kg.

short: A Paris-based intergovernmental body, set up after the 1973 oil shock, that analyses energy markets and coordinates emergency oil stock releases among member countries.
kid: The IEA is like a group of neighbours who keep extra water jugs. If the tap suddenly stops, they share the jugs, and they also keep track of how much water everyone uses.
detail: The International Energy Agency (IEA), based in Paris, was set up in 1974 within the OECD framework after the 1973 Arab oil embargo, to protect oil-importing countries from supply shocks. Members must hold emergency oil stocks equal to at least 90 days of their net imports, and the IEA can coordinate releases: it did so in 1991, 2005, 2011 and twice in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine. Its monthly Oil Market Report and annual World Energy Outlook are closely watched, and changes to its demand forecasts can move oil prices. India has been an IEA Association country since 2017 and keeps strategic petroleum reserves in underground caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur. Confusion to avoid: the IEA speaks for energy consumers, whereas OPEC speaks for producers, and their demand forecasts often clash; it is also different from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), a US government statistics body.
example: IEA members must hold emergency stocks covering at least 90 days of net oil imports. Say a member imports 2 million barrels a day: it must hold at least 90 × 2 million = 180 million barrels.
formula: Minimum emergency stocks = 90 days × Average daily net oil imports

short: Extra oil that producers, mainly Saudi Arabia and the UAE, could pump within 30 days and sustain for 90 days but are holding back.
kid: Imagine a lemonade stand with an extra jug kept in the fridge. If other stands run out, it can pour more right away so nobody goes thirsty.
detail: Spare capacity is the oil production that can be brought online within 30 days and sustained for at least 90 days, as defined by the US Energy Information Administration. Almost all of it sits with OPEC+ Gulf producers, chiefly Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which deliberately pump below capacity; US shale producers hold almost none. It works as the world's shock absorber: when war, hurricanes or sanctions knock supply out, spare capacity can replace it. When the cushion is thin, as in 2008 and 2022, even small disruptions cause price spikes, while a thick cushion caps rallies. OPEC+ cuts in 2023 and 2024 built a large cushion, which the group began releasing in 2025. For India, which imports over 85% of its crude, it is a key safeguard. Confusion to avoid: spare capacity is unused ability to produce, not oil in storage like strategic reserves.
example: Say a producer can sustainably pump 12 million barrels a day but is producing 9 million. Its spare capacity is 12 - 9 = 3 million barrels a day, enough to replace a 2 million barrel-a-day outage elsewhere with 1 million to spare.
formula: Spare capacity = Sustainable production capacity - Current production

short: The gap between what Indian state-run fuel retailers would charge at market-linked prices and the lower prices they actually charge, often at government urging.
kid: Imagine your lemonade costs you 10 coins to make, but you are told to sell it for 8 coins. The 2 coins you miss on each cup is the missing money.
detail: An under-recovery is the gap between the market-linked price a fuel would fetch and the lower price at which India's state-run oil marketing companies (IOC, BPCL and HPCL) actually sell it. The market price is usually an import-parity or trade-parity price: what the fuel would cost landed in India, including freight, insurance and duties. It is a notional figure based on a benchmark price, not an accounting loss, since actual costs and refining profits differ. Petrol and diesel prices were officially freed in 2010 and 2014, yet the companies have often held pump prices steady when crude spiked, as in 2022, and recouped later. Domestic LPG is the main remaining source, and the government has compensated the companies with one-off grants, including ₹22,000 crore in 2022 and ₹30,000 crore approved in 2025. Confusion to avoid: an under-recovery is not a subsidy, which is cash the government actually pays.
example: Say the import-parity cost of a 14.2 kg LPG cylinder is ₹1,000 but it sells for ₹850. The under-recovery is ₹150 per cylinder; on 10 crore cylinders a month, that is ₹150 × 10 crore = ₹1,500 crore a month.
formula: Under-recovery = (Import or trade parity price - Actual realised price) × Volume sold

short: Ageing oil tankers with murky ownership and often no Western insurance, used to move oil from sanctioned countries such as Russia, Iran and Venezuela.
kid: Some ships sail quietly with their lights off and their names hidden, so nobody knows whose they are. They carry oil that some countries said should not be sold.
detail: The shadow fleet is a group of tankers, often more than 15 years old, that move oil from sanctioned countries outside Western shipping and insurance networks. It grew rapidly after December 2022, when the G7 and EU capped the price of Russian seaborne crude, barring Western firms from shipping or insuring oil sold above the cap. Owners hide behind shell companies, register ships under flags of convenience, switch off location transponders, transfer cargoes at sea and often change names. Estimates range from several hundred to over a thousand ships. The fleet keeps sanctioned oil flowing, limiting the effect of sanctions on global supply and prices, and lets refiners in India and China buy discounted crude. Risks include uninsured oil spills and Western sanctions on individual tankers. Confusion to avoid: the price cap restricts Western services, not the purchase of Russian oil itself, so buying it is not automatically illegal.
example: Say a tanker carries 700,000 barrels of crude bought at a $12 discount to Brent. The buyer saves 700,000 × $12 = $8.4 million on the cargo, which is why discounted sanctioned oil keeps finding buyers despite the risks.

short: The price charged to move goods by ship, truck, rail or air, usually quoted per container, per tonne or per day of hiring a ship.
kid: If you want a big truck or ship to carry your toys to a friend far away, you pay for the ride. When many people want rides at once, the ride costs more.
detail: Freight rates are the price of transporting goods, and in markets the term usually means ocean shipping. Container rates, for manufactured goods, are quoted per 20-foot (TEU) or 40-foot (FEU) container and tracked by benchmarks such as the Drewry World Container Index and the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI). Dry bulk rates are tracked by the Baltic Dry Index, and tanker rates in dollars per day or per tonne. Because fleets cannot grow quickly, rates swing wildly: Drewry's index jumped from under $2,000 per 40-foot container before the pandemic to above $10,000 in 2021, and rose sharply again in 2024 when Red Sea attacks forced ships around Africa. Higher freight raises importers' costs, feeds goods inflation with a lag and squeezes exporters, including Indian textile and engineering firms. Confusion to avoid: headline indices show spot rates, while many large shippers pay contract rates fixed for months.
example: Say an exporter in Mumbai ships 10 forty-foot containers to Rotterdam. At $2,000 per container, freight costs 10 × $2,000 = $20,000; if a crisis lifts the rate to $5,000, the bill rises to $50,000, an extra $30,000 for the same goods.

short: Narrow sea routes, such as the Strait of Hormuz or the Suez Canal, through which a large share of world trade must pass.
kid: Imagine lots of children trying to leave a classroom through one small door. If something blocks the door, everyone gets stuck and late.
detail: Shipping chokepoints are narrow passages on major sea routes where traffic concentrates and alternatives are long or costly. The Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and Oman, carries around a fifth of global oil consumption plus much of Qatar's liquefied natural gas. The Strait of Malacca links the Indian Ocean to East Asia, while the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the Red Sea and the Suez Canal form the shortest route between Asia and Europe. From late 2023, Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping forced most container lines to sail around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding about 10 to 14 days and sharply raising freight and insurance costs. A large share of India's oil and gas imports pass through Hormuz, and much of its trade with Europe uses the Red Sea. Confusion to avoid: chokepoints rarely close completely; markets price the risk through oil prices, war-risk insurance premiums and freight rates.
example: Say a ship sailing from Mumbai to Rotterdam via Suez takes 20 days, but diverting around the Cape of Good Hope adds 12 days. At a charter cost of $40,000 a day, the detour adds 12 × $40,000 = $480,000, before extra fuel.
